domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's primary object is the agent loop and harness architecture, including migration from LangGraph to a custom Effect-TS loop, A2A protocol, human-in-the-loop tool approval, and tools-and-skills pattern. OpenGov is an ERP software company serving thousands of state and local governments with budgeting, procurement, asset management, and permitting products. The presentation covers building the agent loop, running agents in production, and scaling across thousands of government customers with observability and iteration. Prerequisites include TypeScript knowledge and familiarity with schema validation libraries like Zod, indicating an intermediate engineering audience. A hands-on conference presentation at the AI Engineer conference with live demonstrations and code examples. All cited evidence anchors are graded 'said_in_transcript' with direct excerpts from the talk.

summary: Gabe De Mesa, a software engineer on OpenGov's AI agents team, presents the architecture and production practices behind OG Assist, an AI agent integrated across OpenGov's ERP product suite serving thousands of state and local governments with budgeting, procurement, asset management, and permitting software. OG Assist enables first-party agent experiences where agents make tool calls to look up suite-specific data, see and act on screen content, and highlight UI elements for users. The team bet on Effect, an open-source TypeScript library providing schema validation, error handling, logging, tracing, and structured concurrency, migrating from LangGraph to a custom Effect-native agent loop for full control over complex use cases, fine-grained tracing, and dependency injection for hot-swapping language models. For agent intercommunication, they adopted Google's A2A protocol with agent cards as rigorous contracts between front-end and back-end. Feedback combines thumbs-up/down signals with automated CI evals testing real completions against expected tool usage. Human-in-the-loop features deterministically interrupt the agent loop for tool call approval on mutating operations. Sandboxing provides ephemeral, isolated environments for agent code execution with automatic teardown. Rolling summarization manages long context by maintaining running summaries after N messages with only recent messages in context, plus a memory recall component. Generative UI allows agents to render forms and UI elements at runtime, creating personalized, in-the-moment experiences. Effect provides tracing and observability out of the box with automatic span tagging, enabling bottleneck profiling and cross-service failure correlation critical for agentic systems. The team's philosophy is that tools and skills are all you need—building tools with Effect's toolkit pattern and registering them with language models. Internally, OpenGov uses Claude and Cursor to accelerate code reading, writing, review, and shipping, building internal tools and skills alongside customer-facing ones. The presentation emphasizes shipping as the start of iteration, not the finish.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Agenda
sections.summary: Gabe introduces himself as an OpenGov engineer on the AI agents team and outlines the agenda: OG Assist overview, origin story, Effect bet, core agent loop, A2A protocol, evals, sandboxing, long context, monitoring, feedback, tools and skills, and internal AI usage for development workflows.

sections.title: About OpenGov and OG Assist
sections.summary: OpenGov is a 14-year-old ERP software company serving thousands of state and local governments with budgeting, procurement, asset management, and permitting products. OG Assist is a button in the navigation bar across all product suites, powered by tools and skills built by each product team. Demonstrated with a utility billing example where the agent looks up rate codes via tool calls.

sections.title: Origin Story
sections.summary: A principal spun up the new AI agents team as AI took off, and Gabe joined immediately. OG Assist grew and was integrated into all products, both backend and frontend. The agent can see what's on screen, take action on page elements, and highlight clickable next steps for users.

sections.title: The Big Bet on Effect
sections.summary: The team bet on Effect, an open-source TypeScript library that helps write better code with schema (similar to Zod), error handling, logging, traces, and structured concurrency. It has paid off in dividends for architecture, service creation, and the core agent loop design.

sections.title: Effect Native Loop
sections.summary: Originally on LangGraph, the team migrated to a custom Effect-native agent loop for full agency over the loop, enabling fine-grained control of tracing, structured concurrency, and logging. They use the Effect AI package with chat and language model abstractions, supporting dependency injection for hot-swapping models.

sections.title: A2A Protocol
sections.summary: The team adopted Google's A2A protocol for agent intercommunication, using agent cards (name, description, metadata) as a rigorous spec driving front-end and back-end alignment. A2A extensions support metadata and A2UI capabilities. This protocol has been very helpful for development alignment.

sections.title: Feedback and Evals
sections.summary: Philosophy: shipping is the start, not the finish. They collect feedback via thumbs up/down and also accept calls and emails. Automated evals run in CI against real completions to test whether prompts hit expected tools and behave correctly. Both signals drive rapid iteration on tools, skills, and harness.

sections.title: Humans in the Loop
sections.summary: The team built a feature that deterministically interrupts the agent loop when a tool call requires human approval, showing an accept/reject UI. This builds trust and ensures safety, especially for mutating operations, keeping humans in the driver's seat.

sections.title: Sandboxing
sections.summary: Agents get on-demand ephemeral sandboxes for writing code, executing code, and creating files in a safe, isolated space. Sandboxes are torn down after use. Demonstrated with an agent creating a PDF for the AI Engineer Conference 2026 inside a sandbox.

sections.title: Long Context
sections.summary: Legacy models hit token limits and context overload in long conversations. Rolling summarization proved more effective than stuffing all messages—maintaining a running summary after N messages with only N-5 or N-10 most recent messages in context. A memory component enables recall over summaries for references to earlier conversation topics. This approach has worked well for the team.

sections.title: Generative UI
sections.summary: Agents can render UIs on the fly at runtime. Demonstrated with an agent building a form with essay topic options when asked to generate a long essay. The agent had a form primitive registered and generated options at runtime, creating a personalized, in-the-moment experience.

sections.title: Tracing and Observability
sections.summary: You can't scale what you can't see. Effect provides tracing out of the box—functions are automatically tagged with spans that feed into traces for drill-downs of function calls. Traces show API-to-endpoint-to-handler flows with timing profiles to identify bottlenecks. Failures can be cross-referenced across services, which is critical for agentic systems integrating with other teams and APIs.

sections.title: Tools and Skills
sections.summary: The team believes tools and skills are all you need. Effect provides building blocks: define a tool, add it to a toolkit (collection of tools), and register the toolkit with the language model. Demonstrated with a dad joke tool example. This pattern has paid off wonderfully for the organization and is recommended for others.

sections.title: Developer Velocity and Closing
sections.summary: OpenGov uses agents internally as well as for customers. Claude and Cursor have been game-changers for accelerating code reading, writing, review, and shipping. The team builds internal tools and skills alongside customer-facing ones. Gabe closes by encouraging the audience to build agents that ship to production.
